claims.text: WTaTiVZr has superior plastic strain relative to commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
WTaTiVZr has superior toughness relative to commercially pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
Fine-scale precipitates or dispersoids form in situ at WTaTiVZr grain boundaries during high-temperature exposure.
Grain-boundary precipitates or dispersoids govern the alloy's plastic strain and toughness.
The grain-boundary features improve dislocation mobility.
The grain-boundary features enable grain-boundary sliding.
The grain-boundary features blunt crack tips during high-temperature deformation.
Pure tungsten has a more homogeneous microstructure than the proposed precipitate-containing WTaTiVZr alloy.
Pure tungsten exhibits limited plastic strain under comparable high-temperature conditions.
Pure tungsten exhibits lower fracture toughness than WTaTiVZr under comparable high-temperature conditions.
Pure tungsten's limited plastic strain and lower toughness are caused by its homogeneous microstructure and lack of grain-boundary precipitates or dispersoids.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate approximately from 900 to 1500 °C under inert or vacuum conditions.
The mechanism may not operate at lower temperatures.
The mechanism may not operate after processing that fails to form or stabilize the grain-boundary precipitates or dispersoids.
The magnitude of plastic-strain and toughness improvements depends on precipitate or dispersoid nature, density, and distribution.
The magnitude of the mechanical improvements depends on processing variables.
Matched high-temperature tensile and fracture-toughness testing of WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten can test the predicted mechanical differences.
Microscopy and dislocation measurements can test whether grain-boundary features correlate with the predicted mechanical improvements.
